prompt.context: Milk & Cheese, Inc. (MCI) is a leading producer of dairy, ham and sausages in the US. Currently, it produces more than 1,000 products. MCI and two competitors dominate this market.
prompt.question: MCI wants to increase its profits. It has hired your firm to help on this matter. How would you approach the problem?

clarifying_info.q: Is MCI interested in acquiring a competitor or expanding overseas?
clarifying_info.a: No, MCI is not interested in acquiring a competitor or expanding overseas.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average volume across products?
What is the average margin across products?
Is SG&A affected by any potential product changes?
clarifying_info.a: SG&A is not affected by the potential changes.

exhibits.title: Margin vs. Volume Scatter Plot
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot of MCI's 1,000+ products with margin on one axis and volume on the other, allowing products to be grouped into quadrants based on average margin and average volume.
exhibits.data: Axes represent margin (%) and volume (tons); average volume = 35k tons; average margin = 16%

exhibits.title: 80/20 (Pareto) Chart with Quadrant Analysis
exhibits.shows: A cumulative profit chart (Pareto) and a four-quadrant breakdown of products labeled A, B, C, D in zones I and II, where zone I represents high-contribution products and zone II represents low-contribution products.
exhibits.data: 80% of profit comes from 20% of products; four quadrants labeled A, B, C, D; zones I and II; approximately 200 products in zone D / category II

framework: Profitability: Revenue Streams (price, volume, product mix) and Costs (COGS, SG&A)
Revenue analysis: break down by product category and identify top/bottom contributors
Cost analysis: compare COGS per product line; SG&A (handled by another team)
Portfolio rationalization: use margin vs. volume analysis to identify low-contribution products
Identify and evaluate alternatives for underperforming products (discontinue, sell, invest)

questions.prompt: How would you approach analyzing which products MCI should stop producing or selling?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that with 1,000+ products a spreadsheet or visual chart is needed. Best approach: scatter plot of margin vs. volume (or margin vs. revenue). Candidate should propose using averages as axis thresholds to create four quadrants, or apply 80/20 (Pareto) logic. Strong candidates will ask for the scatter plot and then independently draw the quadrant lines using the average margin (16%) and average volume (35k tons).

questions.prompt: Given the scatter plot and the quadrant/Pareto analysis, what conclusions can you draw and what should MCI do?
questions.guidance: Zone I (above average on at least one dimension) = important products to retain. Zone D / Category II (below average margin AND below average volume) = approximately 200 products that contribute minimally to profit and are candidates for removal. Candidate should conclude: 'Based on our analysis, there are at least 200 products that are not bringing relevant contribution to MCI profit. MCI should consider selling these products to minor competitors, or simply stopping production if selling to competitors represents a major risk.' Strong candidates will also suggest alternatives such as empowering the product, analyzing growth potential, or repositioning.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternatives does MCI have for products identified as low-margin and low-volume?

categories.name: Discontinue
ideas: Stop production entirely to free up manufacturing capacity
Reduce SKU complexity and streamline operations

categories.name: Divest / Sell
ideas: Sell product lines to smaller regional competitors
License the brand to a third party

categories.name: Invest / Turnaround
ideas: Invest in marketing to grow volume for products with decent margins
Reformulate product to reduce COGS and improve margin
Bundle low-volume products with high-velocity products

categories.name: Risk Considerations
ideas: Selling to a major competitor could jeopardize MCI's market position
Discontinuing products may affect retail shelf space and customer relationships
Supply chain disruption from sudden volume reduction

recommendation: MCI should focus its portfolio by eliminating approximately 200 products that fall below average in both margin and volume (Zone D / Category II).
These products contribute disproportionately little to total profit and consume resources that could be redirected to higher-performing lines.
risks: Selling underperforming products to major competitors could strengthen rivals and jeopardize MCI's competitive position; prefer sale to minor competitors or simple discontinuation.
Rapid portfolio reduction may create short-term capacity underutilization and relationship friction with distribution partners.
next_steps: Conduct detailed product-level P&L review to confirm margin and volume figures for all ~200 target products.
Evaluate sale vs. discontinuation options on a product-by-product basis, factoring in competitive risk.
Develop a phased wind-down plan to minimize supply chain and retailer disruption.
